summary: The note describes the growth of urban gardening and local food production, especially since September 2023, and how it builds community, supports education, creates small businesses, aids mental health, feeds people in need and benefits the environment. It illustrates each theme with examples such as the Eastside Neighborhood Garden, SkyGreens, Green Minds and Bountiful Harvest. It concludes that urban gardens are reimagining city life and food systems through collective action.
one_line: Urban gardening since late 2023 is strengthening communities, education, local business, mental health, food security and the environment in cities.
key_facts: Urban agriculture has grown significantly in recent years, notably since September 2023, ranging from patio planters to sprawling community gardens.
Alicia Martinez, a retired school teacher, coordinates the Eastside Neighborhood Garden, which was once a littered vacant lot that many avoided.
On November 5, 2023, urban agricultural expert James O'Connor led a workshop on setting up high-yield vertical gardens in tight spaces.
James O'Connor says urban gardening "turns passive consumers into active food citizens" and can improve air quality and reduce the urban heat island effect.

Alexander Thompson, a former chef turned school garden coordinator, runs a program at Lincoln Elementary that, as of December 2023, improved students' nutrition knowledge and encouraged ownership of the local ecosystem.
School gardens have sprouted up across many districts since the start of the 2023 academic year.
Sarah and Kevin Jacobs launched 'SkyGreens', an urban farm that began on their rooftop and grew into a community-supported agriculture (CSA) program.
Since opening in October 2023, SkyGreens has been selling out weekly produce baskets and is exploring partnerships with local restaurants.
In summer 2023, the Green Minds project, which offers therapeutic gardening sessions, showed significant positive impacts on participants dealing with stress and mental health challenges.
Veronica Singh, a psychologist, volunteers with the Green Minds project.
'Bountiful Harvest' connects urban gardens with food distribution centers, and food banks increasingly rely on its donations.
In November 2023, Bountiful Harvest celebrated a milestone as urban gardens' contributions topped 10,000 pounds of fresh produce donated to food banks across the city.
Urban gardens attract pollinators, combat soil erosion, provide urban wildlife habitats and help filter rainwater, easing the strain on city drainage systems.
Gardens act as living laboratories for rainwater harvesting, composting and non-toxic pest control, which residents often adopt in other parts of their lives.
